full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: In this Rule Nisi the writ petitioner challenges the direction given by the learned Subordinate Judge (respondent No.4) in his judgment and decree dated 16-4-1990 (Annexures D and F to the Writ petition) passed in Money Suit No. 2 of 1989 to respondent No. 2 to recover Taka 16,000 with interest from 19-4-1989 from the writ petitioner. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties and on consideration of evidence, both oral and documentary, decreed the suit in part by the judgment and decree dated 16-4-1990 for Taka 1500 to be realised from respondent No. 5 and also directed the bank authority (respondent No. 2) to realise Taka 16,000 from the Writ petitioner with interest. The learned Subordinate Judge while decreeing the suit came to the definite finding that the writ petitioner misappropriated Taka 16,000 deposited by respondent No. 5 on 18-4-1984. 

 6. The writ petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid direction given in the judgment and decree obtained the Rule Nisi from this Court. 

 7. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, learned Advocate appearing for the writ petitioner, submitted that the Writ Petitioner was neither a plaintiff nor a defendant in the suit and. as such, the Court passed the decree against him without any basis. He further submitted that without giving the petitioner any opportunity to controvert the allegation, the Court directed the bank authority (respondent No. 2) to realise Taka 16,000 from the writ petitioner. He further submitted that the principle of natural justice had been violated by not giving any opportunity to the writ petitioner to explain his position. 

 8. Mr Shamsuddin Babul, learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 2, on the other hand supported the finding and direction given by the learned Subordinate Judge. He submitted that the writ petition was not maintainable as the writ petitioner could avail alternative remedy by way of filing an appeal against the direction given by the learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment and decree. He also submitted that the question of violation of natural justice did not arise as the writ petitioner was examined as PW 2 and given the opportunity to explain his position before the Court. He lastly submitted that the decree was passed in 1990 and the Writ petition was filed in 1996 and as such, on the ground of inordinate delay the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. 

 10. The learned Advocate for respondent No. 2 submitted that this Writ petition was not maintainable as the writ petitioner had alternative efficacious remedy by way of filing an appeal against the direction given in the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. 

 11. If anybody is aggrieved by the judgment and decree, he can file an appeal although he is not a party in the suit. In this respect reliance may be made in the case of HM Saya & Co vs Wazir Ali Industries Ltd and Habib Bank Ltd 21 DLR (SC) 50. 

 "Section 96 of the Civil Procedure Code deals with appeals from decrees and section 104 deals with appeals from orders. These provisions do not in terms say who is entitled to prefer an appeal. The Code, however, lays down that it is the decree or the order that has to be appealed against. If the decree or order appealed from adversely affects a person he should be permitted to challenge the same in appeal even if he was not made a party to the original suit or proceeding." 

 12. The decision given in the case referred to above is applicable in the present case. So, we hold that this Writ petition is not maintainable. Moreover, from Annexure-A to the Writ petition, we find that the Writ petitioner came to learn about the passing of the judgment and decree on 16-4-1990 but he filed the Writ petition in 1996. So, on the ground of inordinate delay this Writ petition is liable to be rejected, in this connection reliance may be made in the case of Sarwarjan Bhuiyan vs Bangladesh 44 DLR 447. The relevant portion of the judgment of the above case is as follows: 

 14. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the Writ petitioner was neither a plaintiff nor a defendant in the suit and, as such, no decree could be passed against him. From the decree we find that the suit was decreed in-part for Taka 1500 only against respondent No. 5 but in the order portion of the judgment as well as in the decree the learned Subordinate Judge directed the bank authority (respondent No. 2) to realise Taka 16,000 with interest from the Writ petitioner, So, it cannot be said that decree was passed against the Writ petitioner. As such, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is misconceived.
